screens.title: Securing Device Access and Management
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why device access is the first line of defense for any network and the practical steps to harden routers and switches. We start with the AAA framework—Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting—and why each piece is essential to safe operations. You will see how local accounts are used for initial access or emergency fallback, and how remote AAA servers centralize control in larger environments. Then we’ll walk through how to enforce secure management protocols, specifically generating RSA keys for SSHv2 and enabling HTTPS for web management while disabling insecure Telnet and HTTP. I’ll also point out common mistakes that lock admins out or expose credentials, such as forgetting to configure local fallback or leaving default servers enabled. By the end you’ll understand how to combine configuration commands into a safe deployment pattern: local fallback, strong RSA keys, VTY access restricted by ACL, and remote TACACS+ or RADIUS for scale. As you view the code and cards here, think about your own management network: who needs access, from where, and how will you ensure auditable, encrypted access? That question helps prioritize the configuration choices you’ll practice in the hands-on activity.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Securing Device Access
Securing Device Access and Management
Protect administrative interfaces using AAA, local fallback, and encrypted management protocols.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Why this matters
Administrative interfaces are gatekeepers. An attacker who gains console or VTY access can change routing, remove ACLs, or expose data. AAA and encrypted management protect both credentials and actions.
In this lesson
You will learn AAA theory, configure local accounts and remote AAA groups, generate RSA keys for SSH, enforce HTTPS, and restrict VTY access with ACLs.
Coming up
  • AAA components and why each matters for auditability.
  • Local authentication and safe fallback patterns.
  • TACACS+ vs RADIUS and when to use each.
  • SSH, RSA keys, HTTPS, and VTY ACLs hands-on template.
AAA Framework
Authentication verifies identity. Authorization scopes what commands a user can execute. Accounting records actions for audit trails and troubleshooting.
Secure Protocols
Use SSHv2 and HTTPS. Disable Telnet and HTTP to prevent credential exposure and passive interception of traffic.
Quick config snapshot
hostname R1
ip domain-name cohortia.local
crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 2048
ip ssh version 2
no ip http server
ip http secure-server
Starter tip
Always configure local admin access before enabling remote AAA. Local fallback prevents lockout during AAA outages.
Explore Key Topics
Three quick areas to focus on for this chapter.
AAA Basics — Understand authentication, authorization, and accounting.
SSH & RSA — Generate keys and enforce SSHv2 for CLI security.
VTY ACLs — Restrict who can even attempt management access.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Safety
screens.narratorSegment: These practice objectives will guide what to check while you configure devices. First, always set local administrative credentials before making remote AAA changes so you can recover access if servers are unreachable. In practice that means creating a local admin account and configuring the console line to accept local logins. Second, when you enable remote AAA, include a local fallback in your authentication and authorization commands so the device will authenticate against its username database if the server group fails. Third, verify RSA key sizes and SSH version: use RSA 2048 or larger and enforce IP SSH version 2 to avoid known protocol weaknesses. Finally, test access control by applying a management ACL to VTY lines that only permits your management subnet; then attempt connections from inside and outside that range. These steps reduce the chance of accidental lockout, credential exposure, or broad access that attackers can use. As you perform hands-on configuration, follow a checklist: local account, secure protocols, server groups with local fallback, and VTY restrictions. This checklist keeps changes recoverable and auditable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Practice & Safety
Checklist for safe changes
  • Local admin first: Create a local admin account and enable login local on the console before changing remote AAA settings.
  • Local fallback: Append the local keyword to AAA commands so the device can authenticate locally if servers fail.
  • Encrypted protocols: Generate RSA keys with 2048-bit modulus and set ip ssh version 2.
  • VTY access control: Apply an access-class that limits management to your subnet.
  • Disable insecure services: Turn off Telnet and HTTP, and enable HTTPS and SSH only.
Common mistakes
Forgetting a console password, omitting local fallback, using weak RSA keys, or leaving HTTP/Telnet enabled. Any of these can expose credentials or lock administrators out during outages.

screens.title: AAA: Authentication, Authorization, Accounting
screens.narratorSegment: AAA is the foundational security framework that governs administrative access to network devices. Authentication answers the question "who are you"—typically via a username and password or a credential from a remote server. Authorization answers "what can you do"—it determines whether a user can enter privileged EXEC mode or run specific commands. Accounting provides an audit trail: who logged in, when, how long they were connected, and which commands they executed. Together these three functions let you both enforce least privilege and investigate incidents after the fact. For example, when a senior engineer needs to change a routing policy, TACACS+ can authenticate their identity, authorize only the specific commands allowed for that role, and record the exact configuration commands in accounting logs. A common misconception is to treat AAA as only authentication; in practice authorization and accounting are equally important for operational security and compliance. If you only authenticate users but do not limit commands or log actions, you still risk misuse and you lose the ability to reconstruct events. As a takeaway, view AAA not as three separate features but as a chain: authenticate the person, authorize their actions, and record those actions for accountability. How would you map these responsibilities in your environment?

keyIdea.text: AAA ensures identity verification, permission control, and activity logging to secure and audit device administration.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › AAA Overview
What AAA means in practice
Use AAA to enforce who can access a device, what they may do, and to record their actions for audits and troubleshooting.
Authentication
Verify identity via local credentials or remote servers.
Authorization
Map users to permitted commands or privilege levels.
Accounting
Record sessions and commands for auditing and incident response.
Key Takeaway

Treat AAA as a single security workflow: identify, permit, and log. Each step reduces risk and helps with compliance.

Concrete example
A network operator authenticates with TACACS+. The device asks the TACACS+ server whether this user can enter privileged mode. The server responds allowing only specific commands. The device sends accounting records of the session for later review.
Common misconception
Believing authentication alone is sufficient. Without authorization and accounting, you cannot enforce least privilege or reconstruct actions after a change.
Check your understanding
Name one scenario where accounting saved time in troubleshooting. How would command authorization have changed the outcome?

screens.title: Configuring Local Authentication Safely
screens.narratorSegment: Local authentication is a simple and essential safety net. When you configure a local user with a secret and apply login local on console and VTY lines, the device can authenticate administrators even if remote servers are unreachable. Start by creating a strong local account using a command that sets a secret; this stores the password hashed. Next, set console line parameters: a console password as a minimal fallback, logging synchronous to reduce console noise, and an exec-timeout to limit idle sessions. For VTY lines, configure transport input to accept only SSH and apply access-class to restrict which hosts can attempt connections. A common mistake is leaving the console without a password or forgetting login local on the console line, which leaves a direct connection unprotected. Another risk is failing to include a local fallback in your AAA definitions later; always configure and test local access before applying remote AAA. In practice, this process reduces the chance of accidental lockout and ensures you have an out-of-band recovery method. After you configure these items, verify by attempting a local console login and an SSH login from allowed and disallowed subnets.

keyIdea.text: Define a local admin, protect console with a password and login local, restrict VTY to SSH, and use an ACL to limit who can attempt management access.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Local Authentication
Step-by-step
  1. Create a local user with a secret and strong password hashing.
  2. Configure console line: logging synchronous, exec-timeout, password or login local.
  3. Configure VTY lines: transport input ssh, login local, access-class with management ACL.
  4. Test local console access and SSH from allowed subnet, verify deny from outside.
Common mistake
Not setting a console password or forgetting login local enables an unprotected path into the device.
Example configuration snippets
username admin secret CohortiaSecurePass!
line console 0
 logging synchronous
 exec-timeout 10 0
 password consolepass
 login local
line vty 0 4
 transport input ssh
 login local
 access-class MGMT_VTY_ACL in
Verification
After saving configuration, attempt an SSH connection from 192.168.10.5 (allowed) and from a host outside the range (should be denied).

screens.title: aaa new-model and the local fallback keyword
screens.narratorSegment: The command to enable the AAA framework on Cisco devices is to turn on the AAA new-model. This switches the device into the AAA configuration mode where authentication, authorization, and accounting commands become available. Once enabled, you can define authentication and authorization methods and point them at remote server groups. Crucially, when you specify authentication or authorization methods you should append a local fallback method. For example, 'aaa authentication login default group TAC_SERVERS local' tells the router to try TACACS+ servers first and then consult the local username database if the servers are unreachable. The local keyword prevents accidental lockout: if you only configured remote servers and they fail, administrators could lose all access to the device. A common misconception is that local fallback is only a convenience; in reality it is a critical safety mechanism. Another pitfall is enabling new-model without verifying that local accounts exist and console lines accept local logins. Always create a tested local admin before enabling AAA new-model and before switching login methods on the VTY and console lines. How will you verify local fallback in your next change window?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › aaa new-model & local
Enable AAA safely
Use aaa new-model to unlock AAA commands, then define authentication and authorization method lists that include local as a fallback.
Example rationale: Remote TACACS+ may be centrally managed and preferred, but network outages or server misconfiguration can make those servers unreachable. The local fallback ensures you can still authenticate using a device-stored account.
Key Takeaway

Always create and test a local admin account first, then enable aaa new-model and configure method lists that include local fallback.

Config pattern
aaa new-model
aaa authentication login default group TAC_SERVERS local
aaa authorization exec default group TAC_SERVERS local
Misconfiguration to avoid: configuring method lists that reference only remote servers without local fallback.
Verification: simulate remote server outage and ensure local credentials still grant access via console or VTY when the device cannot reach servers.

screens.title: TACACS+ Protocol Overview
screens.narratorSegment: TACACS+ is a Cisco-developed protocol that is widely used for device administration because it separates authentication and authorization into discrete operations. When an administrator attempts to log in, the device sends authentication queries to the TACACS+ server over TCP port 49. Once authenticated, the device can ask the server for command authorization decisions. TACACS+ encrypts the entire packet body, which provides stronger protection for command strings and attributes. This separation enables very granular command authorization—useful in large teams where operators have differing permissions. A common practical use is to allow network technicians to view interfaces but require higher-level engineers to execute configuration commands. The architectural benefit is centralized policy and per-command control combined with an encrypted channel over TCP. A misconception is that TACACS+ is always mandatory for small networks; while it provides great control, small deployments often rely on local accounts due to operational simplicity. The key decision is whether you need centralized, per-command authorization and full-packet encryption. If you do, TACACS+ is a strong fit. If not, RADIUS may be sufficient where more lightweight network access control is needed.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › TACACS+
Protocol architecture
TACACS+ runs over TCP port 49, separates authentication and authorization, and encrypts the entire packet body. This provides per-command authorization and stronger confidentiality.
TCP port 49
Full packet encryption
Per-command authorization
Use TACACS+ when you need precise command control and encrypted command content. It integrates well with centralized admin systems and supports granular role-based policies for device management.
Concrete example
A TACACS+ policy can allow a junior operator to show interface status but deny them from changing BGP neighbors. The server logs each command, enabling accountability.
Misconception
TACACS+ is often thought to be required for security. It is powerful, but evaluate overhead and infrastructure before replacing simple local auth in small sites.

screens.title: TACACS+ vs RADIUS
screens.narratorSegment: TACACS+ and RADIUS are both widely used for centralized authentication, but they differ in protocol behavior and typical use cases. TACACS+ uses TCP port 49 and encrypts the entire packet body, which supports granular command authorization and protects command contents. RADIUS is an open standard that typically uses UDP ports 1812 for authentication and 1813 for accounting and encrypts only the user's password in the packet. RADIUS combines authentication and authorization, which makes it a common choice for network access services like 802.1X where speed and wide interoperability matter. The practical decision often depends on whether you need per-command authorization and full packet confidentiality — choose TACACS+ for device administration with fine-grained control, and choose RADIUS where the priority is broad client support and network-access workflows. A frequent misconception is that RADIUS is insecure because it only encrypts passwords; in many access-control scenarios existing protections and transport boundaries make it adequate. The right choice often comes down to existing infrastructure and the level of authorization granularity required. TACACS+ vs RADIUS means use tacacs+ for detailed command authorization and full-packet encryption; use radius where network access and broad interoperability are primary needs.. In practical terms, differences, ports, encryption behavior, and when to choose each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

TACACS+
  • TCP port 49, encrypts entire packet body.
  • Separates authentication and authorization for per-command control.

screens.title: Defining AAA Server Groups and Applying Methods
screens.narratorSegment: When you configure remote AAA, you first enable the AAA new-model and then define server groups that represent collections of TACACS+ or RADIUS servers. For TACACS+, create a group named TAC_SERVERS and add the server IP addresses. Then reference that group in authentication and authorization method lists. A safe pattern is to append local as a fallback. After defining the group and methods, update the console and VTY line login behavior to use the method lists. A frequent misstep is omitting the group reference in the method list or failing to add the local fallback, which creates a single point of failure. Verify the configuration by simulating unreachability of the server and confirming local authentication still works. The code panel here shows the core commands you will use in the lab, and you should type them in the same sequence when configuring a real device. Defining AAA Server Groups and Applying Methods means define server groups and servers, then apply method lists with local fallback and test by simulating server outages.. In practical terms, configure server groups, add servers, and apply authentication and authorization lists. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Enforcing SSH and Generating RSA Keys
screens.narratorSegment: SSH replaces Telnet for secure command-line access. To enable SSH you must set a hostname and an IP domain name so the device can generate unique RSA keys. Generate RSA keys with a strong modulus—2048 bits is the recommended minimum for modern security. After key generation, explicitly set the device to use SSH version 2 which offers improved cryptography and security features. Finally, on VTY lines restrict transport input to ssh so the device will not accept Telnet connections. Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › SSH Enforcement
Minimal SSH setup
hostname R1
ip domain-name cohortia.local
crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 2048
ip ssh version 2
line vty 0 4

Use strong RSA keys, enforce SSHv2, and restrict VTYs so Telnet cannot be used. Test SSH sessions to validate correct operation.
Why modulus size matters
A larger RSA modulus increases the computational work required to break the key. Use at least 2048 bits to balance security and device CPU load. Avoid tiny key sizes that are fast to generate but weak to attack.
Check your understanding
After you generate keys, how would you confirm the device is offering SSHv2 only and refusing Telnet connections?

screens.title: HTTPS, Disabling HTTP & General Management Plane Hardening
screens.narratorSegment: Securing the web-based management plane requires disabling the insecure HTTP server and enabling the secure variant, HTTPS. Use the command to enable the secure-server and remove the plain HTTP server. When HTTPS is enabled, connections are encrypted with TLS, protecting GUI passwords and session data. Also ensure SNMP, if used for management, is configured securely with v3 or proper community restrictions. Beyond protocol selection, harden access by restricting VTY and web management to a dedicated management subnet via access-lists and applying access-class on VTY lines. Avoid setting ip http server or transport input telnet. Another important step is to limit which accounts can access privileged EXEC and to enable accounting so GUI actions are logged. Common mistakes include leaving HTTP or Telnet enabled for convenience or using weak community strings for SNMP. To validate your changes, attempt an HTTP connection and confirm it is refused, then open HTTPS from an allowed management IP and verify you can authenticate. These simple steps dramatically reduce the attack surface for the management plane. HTTPS, Disabling HTTP & General Management Plane Hardening means disable http and telnet, enable https, secure snmp, restrict management subnets, and log management actions for auditability.. In practical terms, enable https, disable http/telnet, and other best practices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Web and protocol commands
no ip http server

Disabling insecure services is as important as enabling secure ones. Confirm plain HTTP is rejected and HTTPS accepts connections from allowed hosts.
Additional best practices
  • Use SNMPv3 or restrict SNMP community strings to management hosts.
  • Log administrative actions and enable accounting where possible.
  • Apply management plane ACLs that only permit known management networks.
Common mistake
Leaving HTTP or Telnet enabled for compatibility. These protocols expose credentials in clear text and should be disabled immediately.

screens.title: VTY Access Control Lists and Access-Class
screens.narratorSegment: Applying an access-class to VTY lines reduces the attack surface by preventing unauthorized IPs from initiating management sessions. The general flow is to define a standard access-list that permits your management subnet and denies others, then apply it to the VTY inbound direction. For example, an ACL that permits 192.168.10.0/24 and denies any other source will ensure only hosts in your management network can even try to start an SSH session. After applying the ACL, test connections from an allowed address and from an external address to confirm the list is enforced. A common misstep is applying overly permissive ACLs or forgetting to include a permit for the management host used for testing, which can appear as a configuration failure. Another pitfall is assuming the ACL allows existing sessions to continue; the ACL only filters new inbound connection attempts. Use descriptive names for access-lists and consider placing them in configuration management change windows because they can block all remote management if misconfigured. As a takeaway, access-class is a low-cost and high-impact control that should be part of every management plane hardening checklist.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › VTY ACLs
Example ACL and application
ip access-list standard MGMT_VTY_ACL

 deny any
!
line vty 0 4

This configuration ensures only hosts from the management subnet may initiate SSH on VTY lines; others are denied before authentication.
Testing and pitfalls
  • Test from an allowed host to confirm access.
  • Test from a denied host to confirm rejection.
  • Avoid locking out changes: keep console access configured and tested.

screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough uses the lab template to configure a secure management posture on Router R1. The exercise begins by entering configuration mode and setting hostname and domain so RSA keys can be generated. Create a local user ‘‘admin’’ with a secret, then configure console settings with logging and an exec-timeout and ensure the console accepts local logins. Next, create a management ACL that permits 192.168.10.0/24 and apply it to VTY lines while restricting transport to SSH. Enable SSHv2 and generate strong RSA keys. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Lab: Secure R1
Starter CLI template (enter on R1)
R1>enable
R1#configure terminal
R1(config)#hostname R1
R1(config)#ip domain-name cohortia.local
R1(config)#crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 2048
  (Press Enter to accept default key name)

R1(config)#username admin secret CohortiaSecurePass!

R1(config)#line console 0
R1(config-line)#logging synchronous
R1(config-line)#exec-timeout 10 0
R1(config-line)#password consolepass
R1(config-line)#login local
R1(config-line)#exit

R1(config)#ip access-list standard MGMT_VTY_ACL
R1(config-std-nacl)#permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config-std-nacl)#deny any
R1(config-std-nacl)#exit

R1(config)#line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)#transport input ssh
R1(config-line)#login local
R1(config-line)#access-class MGMT_VTY_ACL in
R1(config-line)#exit

R1(config)#ip ssh version 2
R1(config)#no ip http server
R1(config)#ip http secure-server

R1(config)#aaa new-model
R1(config)#aaa authentication login default group TAC_SERVERS local
R1(config)#aaa authorization exec default group TAC_SERVERS local

R1(config)#tacacs-server host 10.0.0.1 key CohortiaTACACSKey!
R1(config)#aaa group server tacacs+ TAC_SERVERS
R1(config-sg-tacacs+)#server 10.0.0.1
R1(config-sg-tacacs+)#exit

R1(config)#end
R1#write memory
Lab verification steps
  1. SSH from 192.168.10.x — should authenticate.
  2. SSH from outside the subnet — should be denied by ACL.
  3. Disable reachability to 10.0.0.1 and verify local login still works.
  4. Try HTTP connection to confirm it is refused; confirm HTTPS is available.
Pro tip
Make changes during a maintenance window and keep local console access handy so you can recover from unintended lockouts.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the compact, high-value concepts to carry forward. AAA is a three-part framework: authenticate identity, authorize actions, and account for activity. Local authentication provides a vital fallback and must be configured before enabling remote AAA. TACACS+ is preferred for device administration when you need per-command authorization and full-packet encryption; it operates over TCP port 49. RADIUS is common for network access scenarios, uses UDP ports 1812 and 1813, and encrypts only the password field. For the management plane, always enforce SSHv2 with RSA keys of at least 2048 bits and enable HTTPS while disabling HTTP and Telnet. VTY access should be limited to a management subnet using an access-class ACL. Finally, test your fallback and failure scenarios: simulate remote server failure to confirm local login remains available. These core ideas form a checklist for secure device access and should be applied consistently across routers and switches in the enterprise.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why device access is the first line of defense for any network and the practical steps to harden routers and switches. We start with the AAA framework—Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting—and why each piece is essential to safe operations. You will see how local accounts are used for initial access or emergency fallback, and how remote AAA servers centralize control in larger environments. Then we’ll walk through how to enforce secure management protocols, specifically generating RSA keys for SSHv2 and enabling HTTPS for web management while disabling insecure Telnet and HTTP. I’ll also point out common mistakes that lock admins out or expose credentials, such as forgetting to configure local fallback or leaving default servers enabled. By the end you’ll understand how to combine configuration commands into a safe deployment pattern: local fallback, strong RSA keys, VTY access restricted by ACL, and remote TACACS+ or RADIUS for scale. As you view the code and cards here, think about your own management network: who needs access, from where, and how will you ensure auditable, encrypted access? That question helps prioritize the configuration choices you’ll practice in the hands-on activity.

These objectives describe practical skills you will practice and verify. First, you will explain the AAA framework and identify how Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting work together to protect administrative access and create audit trails. You should be able to describe each component and give a real example of why accounting matters when troubleshooting. Second, you will configure local authentication on Cisco devices. This includes defining local usernames and secrets, applying login methods to console and VTY lines, and understanding the safety of having a local fallback. Third, you will implement remote AAA using TACACS+ or RADIUS. That means defining server groups, pointing the device at server IP addresses, and configuring authentication and authorization methods that fall back to local accounts if needed. Finally, you will secure the management plane—enabling SSHv2 with strong RSA keys, disabling Telnet and HTTP, enabling HTTPS, and restricting VTY access with an ACL. Each objective is focused on hands-on configuration and common mistakes to avoid, so that you can both harden devices and recover safely if servers become unreachable.

These practice objectives will guide what to check while you configure devices. First, always set local administrative credentials before making remote AAA changes so you can recover access if servers are unreachable. In practice that means creating a local admin account and configuring the console line to accept local logins. Second, when you enable remote AAA, include a local fallback in your authentication and authorization commands so the device will authenticate against its username database if the server group fails. Third, verify RSA key sizes and SSH version: use RSA 2048 or larger and enforce IP SSH version 2 to avoid known protocol weaknesses. Finally, test access control by applying a management ACL to VTY lines that only permits your management subnet; then attempt connections from inside and outside that range. These steps reduce the chance of accidental lockout, credential exposure, or broad access that attackers can use. As you perform hands-on configuration, follow a checklist: local account, secure protocols, server groups with local fallback, and VTY restrictions. This checklist keeps changes recoverable and auditable.

AAA is the foundational security framework that governs administrative access to network devices. Authentication answers the question "who are you"—typically via a username and password or a credential from a remote server. Authorization answers "what can you do"—it determines whether a user can enter privileged EXEC mode or run specific commands. Accounting provides an audit trail: who logged in, when, how long they were connected, and which commands they executed. Together these three functions let you both enforce least privilege and investigate incidents after the fact. For example, when a senior engineer needs to change a routing policy, TACACS+ can authenticate their identity, authorize only the specific commands allowed for that role, and record the exact configuration commands in accounting logs. A common misconception is to treat AAA as only authentication; in practice authorization and accounting are equally important for operational security and compliance. If you only authenticate users but do not limit commands or log actions, you still risk misuse and you lose the ability to reconstruct events. As a takeaway, view AAA not as three separate features but as a chain: authenticate the person, authorize their actions, and record those actions for accountability. How would you map these responsibilities in your environment?

Local authentication is a simple and essential safety net. When you configure a local user with a secret and apply login local on console and VTY lines, the device can authenticate administrators even if remote servers are unreachable. Start by creating a strong local account using a command that sets a secret; this stores the password hashed. Next, set console line parameters: a console password as a minimal fallback, logging synchronous to reduce console noise, and an exec-timeout to limit idle sessions. For VTY lines, configure transport input to accept only SSH and apply access-class to restrict which hosts can attempt connections. A common mistake is leaving the console without a password or forgetting login local on the console line, which leaves a direct connection unprotected. Another risk is failing to include a local fallback in your AAA definitions later; always configure and test local access before applying remote AAA. In practice, this process reduces the chance of accidental lockout and ensures you have an out-of-band recovery method. After you configure these items, verify by attempting a local console login and an SSH login from allowed and disallowed subnets.

The command to enable the AAA framework on Cisco devices is to turn on the AAA new-model. This switches the device into the AAA configuration mode where authentication, authorization, and accounting commands become available. Once enabled, you can define authentication and authorization methods and point them at remote server groups. Crucially, when you specify authentication or authorization methods you should append a local fallback method. For example, 'aaa authentication login default group TAC_SERVERS local' tells the router to try TACACS+ servers first and then consult the local username database if the servers are unreachable. The local keyword prevents accidental lockout: if you only configured remote servers and they fail, administrators could lose all access to the device. A common misconception is that local fallback is only a convenience; in reality it is a critical safety mechanism. Another pitfall is enabling new-model without verifying that local accounts exist and console lines accept local logins. Always create a tested local admin before enabling AAA new-model and before switching login methods on the VTY and console lines. How will you verify local fallback in your next change window?

TACACS+ is a Cisco-developed protocol that is widely used for device administration because it separates authentication and authorization into discrete operations. When an administrator attempts to log in, the device sends authentication queries to the TACACS+ server over TCP port 49. Once authenticated, the device can ask the server for command authorization decisions. TACACS+ encrypts the entire packet body, which provides stronger protection for command strings and attributes. This separation enables very granular command authorization—useful in large teams where operators have differing permissions. A common practical use is to allow network technicians to view interfaces but require higher-level engineers to execute configuration commands. The architectural benefit is centralized policy and per-command control combined with an encrypted channel over TCP. A misconception is that TACACS+ is always mandatory for small networks; while it provides great control, small deployments often rely on local accounts due to operational simplicity. The key decision is whether you need centralized, per-command authorization and full-packet encryption. If you do, TACACS+ is a strong fit. If not, RADIUS may be sufficient where more lightweight network access control is needed.

TACACS+ and RADIUS are both widely used for centralized authentication, but they differ in protocol behavior and typical use cases. TACACS+ uses TCP port 49 and encrypts the entire packet body, which supports granular command authorization and protects command contents. RADIUS is an open standard that typically uses UDP ports 1812 for authentication and 1813 for accounting and encrypts only the user's password in the packet. RADIUS combines authentication and authorization, which makes it a common choice for network access services like 802.1X where speed and wide interoperability matter. The practical decision often depends on whether you need per-command authorization and full packet confidentiality — choose TACACS+ for device administration with fine-grained control, and choose RADIUS where the priority is broad client support and network-access workflows. A frequent misconception is that RADIUS is insecure because it only encrypts passwords; in many access-control scenarios existing protections and transport boundaries make it adequate. The right choice often comes down to existing infrastructure and the level of authorization granularity required. TACACS+ vs RADIUS means use tacacs+ for detailed command authorization and full-packet encryption; use radius where network access and broad interoperability are primary needs.. In practical terms, differences, ports, encryption behavior, and when to choose each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you configure remote AAA, you first enable the AAA new-model and then define server groups that represent collections of TACACS+ or RADIUS servers. For TACACS+, create a group named TAC_SERVERS and add the server IP addresses. Then reference that group in authentication and authorization method lists. A safe pattern is to append local as a fallback. After defining the group and methods, update the console and VTY line login behavior to use the method lists. The hands-on template includes specific commands to create a tacacs group, add a server host with a shared key, and set the method lists so the device attempts TACACS+ first and then local. A frequent misstep is omitting the group reference in the method list or failing to add the local fallback, which creates a single point of failure. Verify the configuration by simulating unreachability of the server and confirming local authentication still works. The code panel here shows the core commands you will use in the lab, and you should type them in the same sequence when configuring a real device. Defining AAA Server Groups and Applying Methods means define server groups and servers, then apply method lists with local fallback and test by simulating server outages.. In practical terms, configure server groups, add servers, and apply authentication and authorization lists. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

SSH replaces Telnet for secure command-line access. To enable SSH you must set a hostname and an IP domain name so the device can generate unique RSA keys. Generate RSA keys with a strong modulus—2048 bits is the recommended minimum for modern security. After key generation, explicitly set the device to use SSH version 2 which offers improved cryptography and security features. Finally, on VTY lines restrict transport input to ssh so the device will not accept Telnet connections. A typical flow is: set hostname, set ip domain-name, generate keys using the crypto key command with a 2048 modulus, set ip ssh version 2, and configure transport input ssh on VTY. Misconfigurations include generating weak RSA keys, leaving ip ssh version at default 1, or forgetting to restrict VTY transports, which leaves Telnet enabled. After implementing these steps, verify by attempting an SSH session and confirming the protocol version. Also check that Telnet attempts are refused. This flow ensures credentials are encrypted in transit and reduces exposure to passive eavesdropping of management sessions. Securing the web-based management plane requires disabling the insecure HTTP server and enabling the secure variant, HTTPS. Use the command to enable the secure-server and remove the plain HTTP server. When HTTPS is enabled, connections are encrypted with TLS, protecting GUI passwords and session data. Also ensure SNMP, if used for management, is configured securely with v3 or proper community restrictions. Beyond protocol selection, harden access by restricting VTY and web management to a dedicated management subnet via access-lists and applying access-class on VTY lines. Avoid setting ip http server or transport input telnet. Another important step is to limit which accounts can access privileged EXEC and to enable accounting so GUI actions are logged. Common mistakes include leaving HTTP or Telnet enabled for convenience or using weak community strings for SNMP. To validate your changes, attempt an HTTP connection and confirm it is refused, then open HTTPS from an allowed management IP and verify you can authenticate. These simple steps dramatically reduce the attack surface for the management plane. Applying an access-class to VTY lines reduces the attack surface by preventing unauthorized IPs from initiating management sessions. The general flow is to define a standard access-list that permits your management subnet and denies others, then apply it to the VTY inbound direction. For example, an ACL that permits 192.168.10.0/24 and denies any other source will ensure only hosts in your management network can even try to start an SSH session. After applying the ACL, test connections from an allowed address and from an external address to confirm the list is enforced. A common misstep is applying overly permissive ACLs or forgetting to include a permit for the management host used for testing, which can appear as a configuration failure. Another pitfall is assuming the ACL allows existing sessions to continue; the ACL only filters new inbound connection attempts. Use descriptive names for access-lists and consider placing them in configuration management change windows because they can block all remote management if misconfigured. As a takeaway, access-class is a low-cost and high-impact control that should be part of every management plane hardening checklist.

Here are the compact, high-value concepts to carry forward. AAA is a three-part framework: authenticate identity, authorize actions, and account for activity. Local authentication provides a vital fallback and must be configured before enabling remote AAA. TACACS+ is preferred for device administration when you need per-command authorization and full-packet encryption; it operates over TCP port 49. RADIUS is common for network access scenarios, uses UDP ports 1812 and 1813, and encrypts only the password field. For the management plane, always enforce SSHv2 with RSA keys of at least 2048 bits and enable HTTPS while disabling HTTP and Telnet. VTY access should be limited to a management subnet using an access-class ACL. Finally, test your fallback and failure scenarios: simulate remote server failure to confirm local login remains available. These core ideas form a checklist for secure device access and should be applied consistently across routers and switches in the enterprise.

Keep these three short reminders within reach while you make changes. First, always prepare local administrative access before switching to remote AAA to avoid lockout. Second, prefer TACACS+ when you need fine-grained command authorization and full-packet encryption, and use RADIUS when network access interoperability is the higher priority. Third, enforce SSHv2 with at least 2048-bit RSA keys and enable HTTPS while disabling Telnet and HTTP.
